intelligence.title: Go Grab the Intelligent Board

intelligence.human_view: The player is the first thing people see, so the player is the standard the whole presentation is judged by. A recreated player tells them at the first glance that this is a copy; the actual player tells them this is the real thing, made by the people who make the thing. This is the harvest-first discipline at its sharpest: SN-4285 said put the literal player in the frame instead of linking it; this says put the ACTUAL player in, not a new one built to look like it — linking it was the first miss, rebuilding it was the second, and both misses have the same shape, substituting something near the thing for the thing. Sizing the frame to the player instead of squishing the player into the frame is the same rule in the other direction: the frame serves the player, because the player is the pro object and the frame is its stage. And the transport controls are not decoration — pause, stop, backwards, forwards are what make it a player instead of a picture that happens to move.
intelligence.simple_view: We already have a beautiful board that glows and lifts off the page. We take that same board and put it in the frame, next to the player. One big board holds the words, and inside it sit two smaller boards — three sometimes — so the words are easy to read.
intelligence.grandma_view: Think of a beautiful tray that holds smaller shining dishes. The big board is the tray; the little boards hold the words, two or three at a time, so your eyes rest on one small piece, then the next. When there is no player on the slide, the whole tray is the board, glowing on its own.
intelligence.naya_view: The best version of a thing is usually already built, somewhere in the house. The bar he likes is a screenshot of a bar that already exists; the font he loves is a font already rendering on the Ask Naya page; the certificate's glow is already filed. Redesigning any of them is not improvement, it is loss — the new version is "nowhere close to the same," and he has to say so again. Reuse is not laziness here; it is the discipline: take the thing that already earned his eye, put it where it belongs, and spend the effort on the fit, not on a fresh drawing. The two details carry the lesson in miniature: NAYA beside her picture (not underneath — a placement, not a redesign) and less glow in the middle (restraint, not a new effect).
